verdict.summary: A User Authentication (OAuth 2.0) platform app is self-serve with no Box review, and any Box user can authorize it the same day. The catch is the customer side: enterprises that 'Disable unpublished apps by default' make an admin enable your app first, and listing in Box Integrations (optional) goes through a partner review with no published timeline.

evidence.label: inferred
evidence.note: Create a free developer account, New App > User, tick scopes, add a redirect URI (http://localhost allowed), and run the flow.

timeToProd.assumes: An unpublished OAuth 2.0 app with root_readwrite that reads and writes user files; enterprise customers that block unpublished apps add their own admin approval time, and an Integrations listing adds an unspecified partner review.
timeToProd.waitingOn: No review needed. Per customer: an enterprise admin enabling the app where unpublished apps are disabled.

evidence.label: inferred
evidence.note: Box docs don't require publishing for outside users; they describe listing as a way to reach new users. Admin enablement timing is up to each customer.

prerequisites.item: A Box account with Developer Console access (a free developer account works)
prerequisites.why: Apps are created in the Developer Console; a developer account is the alternative if your enterprise account lacks access.

prerequisites.item: Exact-match redirect URIs: HTTPS, or HTTP for localhost/loopback (any port)
prerequisites.why: Box checks redirect URIs by exact match and rejects non-HTTPS URIs other than localhost.

prerequisites.item: A paid enterprise account and a support ticket for on-request scopes such as enterprise_content
prerequisites.why: Free trial accounts can't request these scopes, and Box approves them case by case.

prerequisites.item: For an Integrations listing: icon, screenshots, short and long descriptions, categories, support info and an Add-button URL
prerequisites.why: These are the Publishing tab fields Box asks for before Submit for Approval.

scopeTiers.impact: Reads (and writes) everything the authorizing user owns or collaborates on. root_readwrite is needed to download files. Enough for most file-reading agents.
Self-serve in the console, but they only work where the customer's Box plan has the feature (e.g. Sign enabled for the enterprise).

evidence.label: sourced
evidence.note: Box's scope page doesn't list a plan requirement for ai.readwrite.

scopeTiers.time: Same day, but only for admin installers
scopeTiers.impact: Selectable in the console, but client-side OAuth apps need an Admin or Co-Admin to authorize for these calls to work.
Box support reviews each request and grants it only when the use case needs it. Paid enterprise accounts only.

steps.title: Get a Box developer account
steps.detail: Sign up for a free developer account, or sign in with an enterprise account that has Developer Console access.

steps.title: Create a User Authentication platform app
steps.detail: Developer Console > New App > User > Create. You can't convert an OAuth 2.0 app to Server Authentication later, so pick deliberately.

evidence.label: tested
evidence.note: The console URL returned 302 to account.box.com/login on 2026-10-20. We did not sign in.

steps.title: Choose minimum scopes
steps.detail: Pick root_readonly for a read-only agent, root_readwrite if it downloads or writes, plus ai.readwrite only if calling the Box AI API. Avoid admin and on-request scopes unless needed.

steps.title: Configure scopes, redirect URIs and CORS
steps.detail: On the Configuration tab tick the scopes, add exact redirect URIs (HTTPS, or http://localhost), and add CORS domains only if the browser calls the API.

steps.title: Implement the authorization code flow
steps.detail: Redirect to https://account.box.com/api/oauth2/authorize?response_type=code&client_id=...&redirect_uri=...&state=.... Exchange the code with the client secret at POST https://api.box.com/oauth2/token. Store both tokens per user.

evidence.label: sourced
evidence.note: Endpoints confirmed by live checks (authorize 200, token returned invalid_client for a bogus request).

steps.title: Handle single-use refresh tokens
steps.detail: Access tokens last 60 minutes (expires_in 3600). Each refresh returns a new refresh token and invalidates the old one, valid for 60 days. Persist the new one atomically and serialize refreshes per user.

steps.title: Add 429 back-off
steps.detail: Honor retry-after on 429 rate_limit_exceeded and back off exponentially. Budget 1000 requests/min per user, 240 uploads/min per user, and search caps of 60/min per user and 12/s per enterprise.

steps.title: Write admin-enablement instructions for enterprise customers
steps.detail: Draft a help page telling Box admins how to enable the app: Admin Console > Integrations > Platform Apps Manager > User Authentication Apps, then the More menu. Include your client ID and the scopes used.

steps.title: Go live with outside users
steps.detail: Share your connect link. Users in enterprises that allow unpublished apps can authorize immediately; others ask their admin to enable it.

evidence.label: inferred
evidence.note: No Box step is documented between creating the app and outside users authorizing it.

steps.title: Optional: submit to Box Integrations
steps.detail: Publishing tab > confirm the checklist > fill categories, descriptions, screenshots, icon, support info > Preview > Submit for Approval. Questions go to integrate@box.com.

steps.title: Optional: Box Partner review
steps.detail: The Box Partner team reviews 'as soon as possible'. Box publishes no timeline.

agentCanDo: Pick least-privilege scopes and draft the console configuration
Implement the code flow with state checking and per-user token storage
Add retry-after and exponential back-off for 429s
Write admin-enablement instructions and the Integrations listing copy
humanMustDo: Create the developer account and sign in to the Developer Console
Create the User Authentication app and set scopes and redirect URIs
File a support ticket for any on-request scope
Upload screenshots and submit the Integrations listing, if listing

blockers.symptom: Enterprise users see that the app is disabled or blocked by their admin when authorizing
blockers.cause: The customer's enterprise has 'Disable unpublished apps by default' on, or doesn't enable integrations by default.
blockers.fix: The customer's Box admin enables it under Integrations > Platform Apps Manager > User Authentication Apps. Publishing in Integrations may help where 'Enable Integrations by default' is on.

evidence.label: sourced
evidence.note: The exact wording users see wasn't found in the docs.

blockers.symptom: Refresh fails with invalid_grant after working earlier
blockers.cause: A refresh token was reused (they are single-use), or neither token was used for 60 days.
blockers.fix: Always store the newest refresh token and avoid parallel refreshes. After 60 days idle, send the user through authorization again.

evidence.label: sourced
evidence.note: invalid_grant is the standard OAuth error; the exact Box string wasn't confirmed.

blockers.symptom: redirect_uri_mismatch or the authorize page rejects the redirect
blockers.cause: The redirect URI isn't an exact match, or uses http:// on a non-localhost host.
blockers.fix: Register the exact URI on the Configuration tab and send it unchanged.

evidence.label: sourced
evidence.note: Error string inferred from standard OAuth behaviour.

blockers.symptom: 403 insufficient_scope or access denied on admin endpoints
blockers.cause: Admin scopes work only with an Admin or Co-Admin token, and enterprise_content must be granted by Box support.
blockers.fix: Have an admin authorize, or file a support ticket for on-request scopes from a paid enterprise account.

blockers.cause: Search is capped at 60/min per user and 12/s per enterprise; general calls at 1000/min per user.
blockers.fix: Honor retry-after and back off; cache search results.

nuances.text: Access tokens last 60 minutes. Refresh tokens last 60 days and are single-use, so each refresh returns a new pair.
Box Integrations only lists OAuth 2.0 apps. JWT and Client Credentials apps always need explicit admin authorization and get a Service Account, so they're a poor fit for a multi-customer agent.
The OAuth token acts as the user, so the agent sees only content that user owns or collaborates on. Files the app creates land in that user's account.
Box runs a hosted MCP server at https://mcp.box.com using OAuth. An agent may be able to use it instead of a custom integration.

evidence.label: tested
evidence.note: https://mcp.box.com returned HTTP 401 without a token on 2026-10-20, consistent with an OAuth-protected endpoint.

nuances.text: Box doesn't publish an OIDC discovery document; this is plain OAuth 2.0, not Sign in with Box via OIDC.
